This page contains an active bibliography of scholarly articles, books, and resources that inform and complement the research presented on AffineDrift. Each entry includes a descriptive blurb explaining its relevance to our work.

The resources below span multiple disciplines: nonlinear control theory, biomechanics, motor control, and golf research. They represent foundational works, recent advances, and practical applications that contribute to our understanding of the golf swing as an affine controllable system.

title: Reading List
text:
2 Control Theory & Nonlinear Dynamics

2.1 Khalil, H. K. (2002). Nonlinear Systems (3rd ed.). Prentice Hall.
Description: A comprehensive textbook on nonlinear control systems, covering stability analysis, feedback linearization, and the mathematical foundations of control-affine systems. Essential reading for understanding the theoretical framework underlying our golf swing model.
Relevance: Provides the mathematical rigor for understanding control-affine systems of the form \(\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x)u\), which directly applies to modeling the golf swing dynamics.


2.2 Sastry, S. (1999). Nonlinear Systems: Analysis, Stability, and Control. Springer.
Description: Advanced treatment of nonlinear control theory with emphasis on geometric methods and differential geometry. Includes detailed analysis of underactuated systems and trajectory optimization.
Relevance: The golf swing is fundamentally underactuated—not all degrees of freedom can be directly controlled. This text provides tools for analyzing such systems.

title: Reading List
text:
3 Biomechanics & Motor Control

3.1 Winter, D. A. (2009). Biomechanics and Motor Control of Human Movement (4th ed.). Wiley.
Description: Comprehensive introduction to biomechanics with emphasis on human movement analysis. Covers kinematic and kinetic analysis, muscle mechanics, and coordination patterns.
Relevance: Provides the biomechanical foundation for understanding how joint torques translate to motion in the golf swing kinematic chain.


3.2 Latash, M. L. (2012). Fundamentals of Motor Control. Academic Press.
Description: Explores motor control from a systems perspective, examining how the nervous system coordinates complex movements. Discusses synergies, coordination patterns, and the role of constraints.
Relevance: The golf swing requires precise coordination of multiple joints. This text helps understand how such coordination emerges from neural control and mechanical constraints.

title: Reading List
text:
4 Golf-Specific Research

4.1 Nesbit, S. M. (2005). A three-dimensional kinematic and kinetic study of the golf swing. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine, 4(4), 499-519.
Description: Detailed kinematic and kinetic analysis of the golf swing using motion capture and force plate data. Provides empirical data on joint angles, velocities, and ground reaction forces.
Relevance: Offers quantitative data on actual golf swing dynamics, which can be compared against our theoretical predictions and used to validate models.


4.2 MacKenzie, S. J., & Sprigings, E. J. (2009). Understanding the role of shaft stiffness in the golf swing. Sports Engineering, 12(1), 13-19.
Description: Investigates how shaft flexibility affects clubhead motion and energy transfer. Uses both experimental and computational approaches.
Relevance: Shaft dynamics are a key component of the golf swing model, representing flexible body dynamics in our control-affine framework.

title: Reading List
text:
5 Lagrangian Mechanics & Multibody Dynamics

5.1 Goldstein, H., Poole, C., & Safko, J. (2002). Classical Mechanics (3rd ed.). Addison-Wesley.
Description: Standard reference on classical mechanics, including detailed treatment of Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations. Essential for deriving equations of motion for multibody systems.
Relevance: The Euler-Lagrange equations form the foundation of our golf swing dynamics model. This text provides the mathematical tools for deriving these equations.


5.2 Featherstone, R. (2014). Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms. Springer.
Description: Computational algorithms for simulating multibody systems, including efficient methods for computing inverse dynamics and forward dynamics. Includes treatment of flexible bodies.
Relevance: Provides algorithms that can be used to implement and simulate our golf swing model computationally.

title: Reading List
text:
6 Optimization & Trajectory Planning

6.1 Betts, J. T. (2010). Practical Methods for Optimal Control and Estimation Using Nonlinear Programming (2nd ed.). SIAM.
Description: Comprehensive guide to solving optimal control problems using nonlinear programming. Includes methods for trajectory optimization and parameter estimation.
Relevance: The golf swing can be framed as a trajectory optimization problem: finding the sequence of muscle activations that maximizes clubhead speed at impact.

title: Reading List
text:
7 Additional Resources

7.1 Online Course: MIT 6.832 Underactuated Robotics
Description: Free online course covering underactuated robotic systems, including control-affine systems, trajectory optimization, and applications to biomechanics.
Relevance: Directly applicable to understanding the golf swing as an underactuated system with control-affine dynamics.

title: AffineDrift
text:
Post 1
Here’s a calculation for a hypothetical scenario I have been considering. The scenario is: what would reverse dynamics tell us for a swing in which force was applied only at one point on the grip, but that point wasn’t the mid hands point.
In reverse / inverse dynamics analysis, what we get is an equivalent force and couple at the mid hands point for any given swing. However, we don’t exert couples, we exert forces. To determine the equivalent force and couple in “forward” dynamics at a point other than the point of application you essentially compute the moment of the force at both the locations and introduce a “couple” that accounts for the difference. This is mathematically valid and the two bodies would behave exactly the same.
What I find interesting is that for a single force that is applied off of the point of analysis in inverse dynamics, the result you would get would be a force and a couple, despite only applying a force.
It is very tempting to see a force and couple from inverse dynamics reported and to think it means that you need to push or pull to match the force component and then to twist on it to match the couple component. Unfortunately I don’t think this is an entirely valid assumption to make.
Obviously a single force never exists on a real golf club, but where we apply force to the club with our hands can change. For example we can pull with the pinky of the left hand or with the forefinger. We can push with the palm of the right hand or through the forefinger. Where these points of force application are relative to the midpoint of the hands are can meaningfully change the interpretation of the results one would get from reverse dynamics.
I’ve also shown an example of how the equivalent couple for a set of forces would change for forces of the same magnitude but applied by different parts of the hands. The equivalent couple here changes by about 15%. (In the calculation positive forces are up and positive torques are clockwise).
Post 2
Here’s some analysis I’ve done regarding how we can evaluate the meaning of the net force and couple that we get from reverse / inverse dynamics analysis. I think it could have some bearing on the alpha debate and can give a bit of framework to help understand how to translate real life implications from calculated values.
Essentially, the reverse dynamics process gives a value of a force and couple at a point on the club. Typically the midpoint. This does not paint a true picture of reality as we do not exert our force at the midpoint in all cases. We exert forces at various points along the club. When we exert force somewhere along the club that is not the midpoint, it is possible to adjust the force and couple from the midpoint to a new force and couple at a different point of interest. This is done by keeping the sum of forces and sum of moments between the two points constant and solving straightforward algebraic equations.
The question then arises of “where should we look at the force and couple?”. I think that a good answer to that question is found with the following method using forward dynamics type reasoning.

Recognizing that there are multiple forces applied to the club on multiple sides, resolve these forces into equivalent forces acting on either side of the shaft. There is a mathematical way of doing this that involves summing the moments of each, but the exact details are not particularly important to this theoretical argument. What is important is that at the end of this process you are left with a force acting on either side of the shaft representing the sum of all forces acting on that side of the shaft after this process.
Break this pair of forces down into a couple and a net force by simple vector addition / subtraction. This will leave you with two equal magnitude forces and the “leftovers” from the process which is the net force. The net force will be at whichever point in which the magnitude of the force was higher between the two vectors.
Recognize that the couple is a “free vector” and can be moved to act anywhere on the body without changing the rotational behavior of the body. The leftover force cannot. Due to this, the equivalent force and couple should be evaluated at this point where the force is left over in the forward dynamics generation of a couple.
Take reverse dynamics data and imagine completing this process in reverse to get back to a set of forces that represents reality as best as possible. To do so you would need information that you don’t have like the distribution of the point of application of forces to the grip.

It would seem that through this we haven’t really done much as we don’t have the data to go backwards from reverse dynamics to parse out the forces that we actually applied to the club. However, we can do two different things despite the limitations - 1. Set general bounds on the error of our assumptions to create a range of possible inputs for a set of reverse dynamics data, and 2. Conduct “what if” analysis.
I have included a calculation of the bounds for the error if the point of application of force moves up and down the grip (first picture), as well as a couple of “what if” scenarios where a set of reverse dynamics data is assumed and comparisons are made between cases where the points of application of force on the club were different (last two pictures).
How I think this would apply to the alpha debate is illustrated in the last picture showing a late downswing position in which reverse dynamics gives us a result of positive moment of force and negative couple. Depending on the magnitude of the moment of force, the couple, and the point of force application, a sign change in the couple at the point of interest is mathematically possible despite reverse dynamics data giving a “negative couple” at the midpoint of the grip.
Is it probable? Probably not. But the numerical values can definitely change.

title: AffineDrift
text:
AffineDrift’s name comes from nonlinear control theory – where we try and use math to tame chaotic systems. A “control-affine” system is one in which a nonlinear system is still “linear” in control. An affine system can be separated into a drift component and an actuated component. In the drift component, the history of the system is expressed as the current state – positions and velocities of every component. These positions and velocities can create forces and torques that are seen in the present. They are echoes from the actions of the past. Marcus Aurelius was right after all.
What are the implications for the practitioner? The present must be understood in terms of the past. History matters. The state of the system plays a large role in what is observed in terms of kinetics in the present. What we do is a combination of what we are doing, and what has already been done.

title: 1 Contributing to AffineDrift
text:
Thank you for your interest in contributing to AffineDrift! This document provides guidelines for contributing to the project.



Report Issues: Found a typo, broken link, or bug? Open an issue
Suggest Resources: Know a great video, paper, or tool related to affine control theory or golf biomechanics? Let us know!
Improve Documentation: Help make guides clearer for beginners
Fix Bugs: Submit pull requests for any issues you find
Enhance Content: Suggest improvements to explanations or add new sections





Fork the repository
Clone your fork:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/AffineDrift.git
Create a branch:
git checkout -b feature/your-feature-name
Make your changes
Test locally
Commit and push
Open a pull request







Use semantic HTML5 elements
Maintain consistent indentation (2 or 4 spaces)
Add comments for complex sections
Ensure accessibility (alt text, ARIA labels)





Use existing CSS variables for colors
Follow BEM naming convention when adding new classes
Keep specificity low
Add comments for non-obvious styles
Test responsive behavior





Write clean, readable code
Add comments for complex logic
Avoid global variables
Test in multiple browsers





Use clear, accessible language
Explain technical terms
Maintain consistent tone
Check spelling and grammar
Cite sources when appropriate






Update documentation if you change functionality
Test thoroughly in multiple browsers
Write a clear PR description:

What changes did you make?
Why did you make them?
How did you test them?

Keep PRs focused - one feature or fix per PR
Respond to feedback from reviewers




When reporting issues, please include:

Description: What’s the problem?
Steps to reproduce: How can we see the issue?
Expected behavior: What should happen?
Actual behavior: What actually happens?
Screenshots: If applicable
Browser/OS: What environment are you using?




When suggesting resources for the Resources page:

Verify the resource is high-quality and relevant
Provide complete information:

Title
Author/Creator
URL
Brief description
Why it’s valuable

Suggest appropriate category:

Video Lectures
Academic Papers/Books
Online Courses
Computational Tools
Helpful Links








Use welcoming and inclusive language
Respect differing viewpoints
Accept constructive criticism gracefully
Focus on what’s best for the community





No harassment, discrimination, or inappropriate content
Keep discussions relevant and on-topic
Assume good intentions





Help beginners learn
Share knowledge generously
Give credit where it’s due





If you have questions about contributing, feel free to: - Open an issue with the “question” label - Reach out via the repository discussions



By contributing, you agree that your contributions will be licensed under the same terms as the project.

Thank you for helping make AffineDrift better! Your contributions, big or small, are greatly appreciated.

title: AffineDrift
text:
AffineDrift’s name comes from nonlinear control theory – where we try and use math to tame chaotic systems. A “control-affine” system is one in which a nonlinear system is still “linear” in control. An affine system can be separated into a drift component and an actuated component. In the drift component, the history of the system is expressed as the current state – positions and velocities of every component. These positions and velocities can create forces and torques that are seen in the present. They are echoes from the actions of the past. Marcus Aurelius was right after all.
What are the implications for the practitioner? The present must be understood in terms of the past. History matters. The state of the system plays a large role in what is observed in terms of kinetics in the present. What we do is a combination of what we are doing, and what has already been done.

text:
Post 1
Here’s a calculation for a hypothetical scenario I have been considering. The scenario is: what would reverse dynamics tell us for a swing in which force was applied only at one point on the grip, but that point wasn’t the mid hands point.
In reverse / inverse dynamics analysis, what we get is an equivalent force and couple at the mid hands point for any given swing. However, we don’t exert couples, we exert forces. To determine the equivalent force and couple in “forward” dynamics at a point other than the point of application you essentially compute the moment of the force at both the locations and introduce a “couple” that accounts for the difference. This is mathematically valid and the two bodies would behave exactly the same.
What I find interesting is that for a single force that is applied off of the point of analysis in inverse dynamics, the result you would get would be a force and a couple, despite only applying a force.
It is very tempting to see a force and couple from inverse dynamics reported and to think it means that you need to push or pull to match the force component and then to twist on it to match the couple component. Unfortunately I don’t think this is an entirely valid assumption to make.
Obviously a single force never exists on a real golf club, but where we apply force to the club with our hands can change. For example we can pull with the pinky of the left hand or with the forefinger. We can push with the palm of the right hand or through the forefinger. Where these points of force application are relative to the midpoint of the hands are can meaningfully change the interpretation of the results one would get from reverse dynamics.
I’ve also shown an example of how the equivalent couple for a set of forces would change for forces of the same magnitude but applied by different parts of the hands. The equivalent couple here changes by about 15%. (In the calculation positive forces are up and positive torques are clockwise).
Post 2
Here’s some analysis I’ve done regarding how we can evaluate the meaning of the net force and couple that we get from reverse / inverse dynamics analysis. I think it could have some bearing on the alpha debate and can give a bit of framework to help understand how to translate real life implications from calculated values.
Essentially, the reverse dynamics process gives a value of a force and couple at a point on the club. Typically the midpoint. This does not paint a true picture of reality as we do not exert our force at the midpoint in all cases. We exert forces at various points along the club. When we exert force somewhere along the club that is not the midpoint, it is possible to adjust the force and couple from the midpoint to a new force and couple at a different point of interest. This is done by keeping the sum of forces and sum of moments between the two points constant and solving straightforward algebraic equations.
The question then arises of “where should we look at the force and couple?”. I think that a good answer to that question is found with the following method using forward dynamics type reasoning.

Recognizing that there are multiple forces applied to the club on multiple sides, resolve these forces into equivalent forces acting on either side of the shaft. There is a mathematical way of doing this that involves summing the moments of each, but the exact details are not particularly important to this theoretical argument. What is important is that at the end of this process you are left with a force acting on either side of the shaft representing the sum of all forces acting on that side of the shaft after this process.
Break this pair of forces down into a couple and a net force by simple vector addition / subtraction. This will leave you with two equal magnitude forces and the “leftovers” from the process which is the net force. The net force will be at whichever point in which the magnitude of the force was higher between the two vectors.
Recognize that the couple is a “free vector” and can be moved to act anywhere on the body without changing the rotational behavior of the body. The leftover force cannot. Due to this, the equivalent force and couple should be evaluated at this point where the force is left over in the forward dynamics generation of a couple.
Take reverse dynamics data and imagine completing this process in reverse to get back to a set of forces that represents reality as best as possible. To do so you would need information that you don’t have like the distribution of the point of application of forces to the grip.

It would seem that through this we haven’t really done much as we don’t have the data to go backwards from reverse dynamics to parse out the forces that we actually applied to the club. However, we can do two different things despite the limitations - 1. Set general bounds on the error of our assumptions to create a range of possible inputs for a set of reverse dynamics data, and 2. Conduct “what if” analysis.
I have included a calculation of the bounds for the error if the point of application of force moves up and down the grip (first picture), as well as a couple of “what if” scenarios where a set of reverse dynamics data is assumed and comparisons are made between cases where the points of application of force on the club were different (last two pictures).
How I think this would apply to the alpha debate is illustrated in the last picture showing a late downswing position in which reverse dynamics gives us a result of positive moment of force and negative couple. Depending on the magnitude of the moment of force, the couple, and the point of force application, a sign change in the couple at the point of interest is mathematically possible despite reverse dynamics data giving a “negative couple” at the midpoint of the grip.
Is it probable? Probably not. But the numerical values can definitely change.

Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
text:
Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing” The left wrist in the golf swing can be modeled as a universal joint with two actuated degrees of freedom (flexion/extension and radial/ulnar deviation) and one constrained degree of freedom (forearm rotation axis). Through forward dynamics simulation in MATLAB Simulink, we demonstrate that universal joints generate constraint torques—passive torques about the constrained axis that arise from the interaction of applied torques, system momentum, and geometric constraints. These constraint torques serve as efficient pathways for force and torque transmission from proximal to distal segments but are inherently variable and uncontrollable. We hypothesize that the angle at which the club is gripped relative to the wrist joint axes fundamentally determines whether these constraint torques are transmitted into high-inertia axes (promoting clubhead speed) or low-inertia axes (increasing face angle variability). This analysis provides a mechanical framework for understanding the widely-taught principle of gripping "in the fingers" versus "in the palm" and may explain why arm and club planes are typically not aligned during the downswing. abstract Introduction Force and torque transmission through multi-segment kinematic chains presents fascinating challenges in both robotics and human movement. In the golf swing, torques generated by large proximal muscles must be efficiently transmitted through multiple joints to ultimately control both the speed and orientation of the clubhead. Understanding the mechanical pathways through which this transmission occurs is critical for optimizing both performance and consistency. Traditional biomechanical analysis focuses on actively generated torques—those produced by muscular contraction about joints with actuated degrees of freedom. However, in constrained multi-body systems, passive constraint forces and torques play equally important roles in force transmission. These constraint forces arise at joints where motion is restricted, serving to maintain kinematic constraints while simultaneously transmitting forces between connected segments. This paper explores constraint torques at the left wrist joint during the golf swing, modeled as a universal joint with two actuated rotational degrees of freedom. We demonstrate that: enumerate
Universal joints generate constraint torques about their constrained axes
These constraint torques provide efficient force transmission pathways
The angle at which the club is gripped determines how constraint torques influence clubhead motion
Grip orientation may fundamentally affect both clubhead speed generation and face angle variability enumerate The Wrist as a Universal Joint The radiocarpal (wrist) joint exhibits two primary degrees of freedom: itemize
Flexion/Extension: Movement in the sagittal plane relative to the forearm
Radial/Ulnar Deviation: Movement in the frontal plane itemize These two rotational degrees of freedom occur about approximately perpendicular axes, making the wrist kinematically similar to a universal joint (U-joint) in mechanical systems. The third rotational degree of freedom—forearm pronation/supination—occurs at the radioulnar joints proximal to the wrist, not at the wrist itself. From a control perspective, muscles can directly generate torques about the flexion/extension and radial/ulnar axes at the wrist. However, rotation about the forearm axis occurs through forearm muscles acting at the proximal radioulnar joint. This configuration is critical: the wrist joint itself has no direct actuation about the forearm rotation axis, making this a constrained rather than actuated degree of freedom at the wrist. Universal Joints and Constraint Torques Mechanical Properties of Universal Joints A universal joint connects two rotating shafts whose axes are perpendicular (or nearly so) and typically intersect. The joint permits rotation about two axes while constraining rotation about a third axis and translation along all axes. This configuration is widely used in mechanical systems—most famously in automotive drive shafts—specifically because of its ability to transmit torque through the constrained rotational axis. The key property of a universal joint is that torque applied about the longitudinal axis of one shaft is transmitted to the longitudinal axis of the connected shaft through constraint torques rather than through actively applied forces. These constraint torques arise because the joint geometry enforces kinematic constraints; when the system attempts to violate these constraints, reaction forces and torques automatically emerge to maintain the constraints. Constraint Torques: Definition and Properties In constrained mechanical systems, the equations of motion can be written in the form: equation M(q)q + C(q,q)q + G(q) = {applied} + {constraint} equation where: itemize
\(q\) represents generalized coordinates (joint angles)
\(M\) is the mass/inertia matrix
\(C\) contains Coriolis and centrifugal terms
\(G\) contains gravitational terms
\(\tau_{applied}\) represents actively applied torques (e.g., from muscles)
\(\tau_{constraint}\) represents constraint torques maintaining kinematic constraints itemize The constraint torques can be expressed using Lagrange multipliers: equation _{constraint} = J^T(q)equation where \(J\) is the constraint Jacobian matrix and \(\lambda\) is the vector of Lagrange multipliers. These constraint torques have several important properties: enumerate
No mechanical work: Constraint torques act in directions where motion is prevented, so they perform no work: \(\tau_{constraint} \cdot q = 0\)
Force transmission: Despite doing no work, constraint torques efficiently transmit forces between segments
Nonlinearity: Constraint torques depend nonlinearly on system configuration, velocities, and applied torques
Uncontrollability: Because they arise from constraints rather than actuation, constraint torques cannot be directly controlled
Variability: The dependence on multiple system states makes constraint torques inherently variable enumerate Constraint Torques in Forward Dynamics Simulation In MATLAB Simulink’s Simscape Multibody environment, joint blocks allow specification of input torques and sensing of output torques. For a universal joint driven by input torques about its two actuated axes, the sensed output torques include three components: align {sensed,x} &= {x,applied} + {x,passive} {sensed,y} &= {y,applied} + {y,passive} {sensed,z} &= {z,constraint} align where: itemize
Subscripts \(x\) and \(y\) represent the two actuated axes (e.g., flexion/extension and radial/ulnar)
Subscript \(z\) represents the constrained axis (forearm rotation)
\(\tau_{passive}\) represents passive dynamic effects (inertial, Coriolis, etc.)
\(\tau_{constraint}\) is the constraint torque about the constrained axis itemize The presence of \(\tau_{z,constraint} \neq 0\) despite no direct actuation about the \(z\)-axis is the signature of constraint torque generation. This torque emerges from the interaction of: enumerate
Applied torques about the actuated axes
System momentum and inertial effects
Joint geometry and constraint equations
Configuration-dependent coupling between axes enumerate Physical Demonstration of Constraint Torque Generation The generation of constraint torques at a universal joint can be demonstrated with a simple physical experiment: enumerate
Grasp your left wrist firmly with your right hand
Actively prevent any forearm rotation (pronation/supination)
With your left hand, simultaneously apply: itemize
Flexion torque (curling palm toward forearm)
Ulnar deviation torque (moving hand toward pinky side) itemize
Observe the rotational force felt by the restraining right hand enumerate The torque felt by the right hand about the forearm rotation axis is a constraint torque. It arises not from any muscular effort to rotate the forearm, but from the simultaneous application of torques about the two perpendicular wrist axes. The right hand must apply an equal and opposite constraint torque to maintain the no-rotation constraint. This demonstration reveals an important principle: constraint torques can be generated through coordinated actuation of permitted degrees of freedom, even though the constrained degree of freedom cannot be directly actuated at that joint. Constraint Torque Transmission in the Golf Swing The Wrist as a Torque Transmission Pathway In the golf swing, torques generated by proximal segments (trunk rotation, shoulder internal rotation, forearm pronation) must be transmitted to the club. The wrist joint, positioned between the forearm and hand, serves as a critical link in this transmission chain. The constraint torque property of universal joints provides an elegant mechanism for this transmission. Torque about the forearm rotation axis (generated by forearm pronation/supination muscles) can be transmitted through the wrist to the hand without requiring wrist muscles to actively generate this torque. The constraint properties of the joint handle the transmission automatically. However, this passive transmission comes with a critical caveat: because constraint torques cannot be directly controlled at the wrist, they inherit all the variability present in the proximal segments that generate them. As noted in discussion of this phenomenon: quote [Constraint torques] are dependent on motion of other components—any rotation or torque in the forearm will directly affect these and there are no degrees of freedom in the wrist to modulate or control any of these torques induced from the forearm axis. It is forced to transmit whatever it receives on the rotational axis.'' quote This creates a control challenge: the wrist transmits constraint torques from proximal segments to the club, but has no mechanism to filter or modulate these torques. Whatever variability exists in forearm motion, trunk rotation, or their interaction will be transmitted directly through the wrist via constraint torques. Variability Accumulation Through the Kinematic Chain The constraint torques measured at the wrist include contributions from variability in: enumerate \item Shoulder motion: Variations in shoulder internal/external rotation timing and magnitude \item Forearm rotation: Variability in pronation/supination velocity and acceleration \item Wrist actuation: Variations in flexion/extension and radial/ulnar deviation torques \item Dynamic coupling: Nonlinear interactions between all segment motions \item System configuration: Dependence on instantaneous joint angles throughout the chain enumerate Because the wrist cannot modulate constraint torques, it effectively acts as a passive transmission mechanism that accumulates variability from all upstream sources. The critical question then becomes: where do these variable constraint torques go? The answer depends critically on the angle at which the club is gripped relative to the wrist joint axes. The Grip Angle Hypothesis Coordinate System Definitions To analyze grip angle effects, we must define coordinate systems for the relevant segments: Wrist coordinate system: itemize \item $x$-axis: Flexion/extension rotation axis (approximately dorsal-palmar direction) \item $y$-axis: Radial/ulnar deviation axis (approximately medial-lateral direction) \item $z$-axis: Constrained axis (approximately aligned with forearm long axis) itemize Club coordinate system: itemize \item Shaft axis: Along the club shaft from grip to clubhead \item Alpha axis: Perpendicular to shaft, in the swing plane (controls in-plane angular motion) \item Beta axis: Perpendicular to shaft, perpendicular to swing plane (controls face rotation) itemize Near impact, when the club shaft is roughly aligned with the forearm, these coordinate systems have a particular relationship. However, the critical parameter is how the hand coordinate system (distal end of the wrist universal joint) aligns with the club coordinate system, which depends on grip position. Case 1: Grip in the Fingers (Deep Grip) When the club is gripped predominantly in the fingers: itemize \item The butt of the club sits below the heel of the palm \item The shaft passes through or near the base of the fingers \item The hand's $z$-axis (emerging from the wrist constraint torques) is approximately perpendicular to the shaft itemize In this configuration, constraint torques transmitted through the wrist's constrained axis are directed approximately along the club's alpha axis—the axis of in-plane rotational motion. The alpha axis has high moment of inertia because it represents rotation that moves the clubhead through its maximum radius of gyration. The angular acceleration produced by a constraint torque $\tau_c$ about the alpha axis is: equation \alpha_{swing plane} = \tau_c{I_{\alpha}} equation where $I_{\alpha}$ is the club's moment of inertia about the alpha axis (typically 0.004-0.006 kg·m² for drivers). Because $I_{\alpha}$ is large, even substantial constraint torques produce relatively modest angular accelerations. More importantly, rotation about the alpha axis produces translation of the clubhead through the impact zone—the very motion we want for generating clubhead speed. The constraint torques are channeled into productive work. Furthermore, face angle is minimally affected by alpha axis rotation near impact (when the shaft is near the ball). The relationship between alpha rotation and face angle change is approximately: equation \Delta \theta_{face} \approx \Delta \alpha \cdot \sin(shaft angle) equation Near impact, shaft angle is small, so $\sin(shaft angle) \approx 0$, making face angle relatively insensitive to alpha axis rotation. Case 2: Grip in the Palm (Shallow Grip) When the butt of the club extends into the palm: itemize \item The butt of the club sits in or near the heel of the palm \item The shaft passes through or above the base of the fingers \item The hand's $z$-axis is more closely aligned with the shaft axis itemize In this configuration, constraint torques transmitted through the wrist are directed more closely along the club's beta axis—the shaft rotation axis that controls face angle. This axis has low moment of inertia (typically 0.0001-0.0002 kg·m² about shaft rotation). The angular acceleration produced by the same constraint torque $\tau_c$ is now: equation \alpha_{face rotation} = \tau_c{I_{\beta}} equation where $I_{\beta} \ll I_{\alpha}$. The ratio is typically: equation I_{\alpha}{I_{\beta}} \approx 20-30 equation This means the same magnitude of constraint torque produces 20-30 times greater angular acceleration when directed into face rotation versus swing plane rotation. Moreover, face rotation directly controls clubface orientation—the variable most critical for shot dispersion. Implications for Speed and Consistency The grip angle hypothesis predicts fundamentally different outcomes for the two grip configurations: Finger Grip (Perpendicular to Shaft): enumerate \item Constraint torques directed into high-inertia alpha axis \item Variable constraint torques produce modest, bounded angular accelerations \item Alpha rotation contributes to clubhead translation and speed \item Face angle remains relatively stable despite constraint torque variability \item Lower control burden: variability is channeled into performance-relevant direction enumerate Palm Grip (Aligned with Shaft): enumerate \item Constraint torques directed into low-inertia beta axis \item Variable constraint torques produce large angular accelerations \item Beta rotation contributes primarily to face rotation, not clubhead speed \item Face angle highly sensitive to constraint torque variability \item Higher control burden: precise coordination required to manage face angle enumerate The fundamental trade-off is between an axis where constraint torques are useful but less variable in their effect (alpha) versus an axis where constraint torques are amplified and directly affect the critical performance variable (beta). Quantitative Example Consider a constraint torque with standard deviation $\sigma_{\tau_c} = 5$ N·m transmitted through the wrist during the downswing. For a finger grip directing this into the alpha axis: align \sigma_{\alpha} &= \sigma_{\tau_c}{I_{\alpha}} = 5 N·m{0.005 kg·m^2} = 1000 rad/s^2 \sigma_{\theta} &\approx \sigma_{\alpha} \cdot \Delta t \approx 1000 \times 0.05 = 50 rad/s align This angular velocity variation in the swing plane contributes to clubhead speed variation but has minimal effect on face angle near impact. For a palm grip directing the same torque into the beta axis: align \sigma_{\beta} &= \sigma_{\tau_c}{I_{\beta}} = 5 N·m{0.00015 kg·m^2} = 33,333 rad/s^2 \sigma_{\omega_{face}} &\approx \sigma_{\beta} \cdot \Delta t \approx 33,333 \times 0.05 = 1667 rad/s align This face rotation rate variation translates directly to face angle variation at impact. Over a 50 ms window near impact: equation \sigma_{face angle} \approx 1667 rad/s \times 0.05 s \approx 83 rad \approx 4.8° equation This example illustrates how identical constraint torque variability produces dramatically different outcomes depending on grip orientation. Connection to Arm-Club Plane Separation An interesting corollary of this analysis relates to the commonly observed separation between arm plane and club plane during the downswing. Many golfers maintain distinct planes for arm swing and club rotation, with the club plane typically more upright than the arm plane in the delivery position. This plane separation may provide a mechanical advantage related to constraint torque transmission. When arms and club are constrained to the same plane (a \"single plane\" swing), the geometric relationship between forearm axis and club shaft is more constrained. Specifically, maintaining the club on the arm plane tends to position the shaft more parallel to the forearm axis throughout the downswing. This geometric constraint effectively creates a palm-grip-like mechanical situation even with a physically correct finger grip. The constraint torques transmitted through the wrist will still be directed more toward shaft rotation simply due to the geometric relationship enforced by the single-plane constraint. By allowing the arm and club planes to separate, the golfer can: enumerate \item Position the club shaft more perpendicular to the forearm axis during delivery \item Maintain alignment between wrist constraint torques and the club alpha axis \item Preserve the mechanical advantages of the finger grip configuration \item Reduce sensitivity of face angle to constraint torque variability enumerate This provides a dynamical explanation—based on torque transmission mechanics—for why \"single plane\" swings may be mechanically disadvantageous, independent of other kinematic or comfort considerations. Mathematical Framework: From Kinematics to Kinetics The Forward-Inverse Dynamics Challenge The investigation of constraint torques emerged from a practical modeling challenge: converting between kinematically-driven and kinetically-driven simulations. In a kinematic simulation, joint angles are prescribed as functions of time: equation q(t) = q_{prescribed}(t) equation The inverse dynamics problem then yields the required torques: equation \tau_{total} = M(q)q + C(q,q)q + G(q) equation However, $\tau_{total}$ includes both actively applied and constraint torques: equation \tau_{total} = \tau_{active} + \tau_{constraint} equation In a kinetic simulation, only the active torques should be specified as inputs: equation M(q)q = \tau_{active} + \tau_{constraint} - C(q,q)q - G(q) equation where $\tau_{constraint}$ emerges automatically from the constraint equations. The challenge is decomposing $\tau_{total}$ into active and constraint components. For a universal joint at the wrist: align \tau_{sensed,x} &= \tau_{active,x} + \tau_{passive,x} \tau_{sensed,y} &= \tau_{active,y} + \tau_{passive,y} \tau_{sensed,z} &= \tau_{constraint,z} align The $z$-component is purely constraint torque (no actuation exists). But the $x$ and $y$ components include passive dynamic terms that arise from motion, not from actuation. Separating these requires detailed knowledge of the system dynamics—exactly the topic addressed in robotics courses on constrained dynamics. Constraint Forces in the Equations of Motion For a holonomic constraint (one expressible as a function of positions): equation \phi(q) = 0 equation The constraint force/torque is: equation \tau_{constraint} = J^T(q)\lambda equation where the constraint Jacobian is: equation J(q) = \partial \partial q equation The Lagrange multipliers $\lambda$ are determined by enforcing the constraint at the acceleration level: equation J(q)q + J(q,q)q = 0 equation For a universal joint constraining rotation about the $z$-axis and all translations, the constraint equations and resulting constraint torques involve complex geometric relationships between segment orientations and the joint constraint structure. Fortunately, MATLAB Simulink computes these constraint torques automatically and provides them as sensed outputs. This removes the burden of manual calculation but requires understanding what these values represent and how they emerge from system dynamics. Implications and Future Directions Testable Predictions The grip angle hypothesis generates several testable predictions: enumerate \item Face angle variability: Golfers using palm grips should exhibit greater face angle variability at impact compared to finger grip users, even with similar overall swing kinematics \item Constraint torque magnitude: Forward dynamics simulations with different grip angles should show that identical applied torques produce different constraint torque distributions depending on grip configuration \item Clubhead speed: For the same applied torques and overall swing kinematics, finger grips should produce higher clubhead speeds due to more efficient channeling of constraint torques into translational motion \item Variability sensitivity: Introducing random noise into applied torques (as in Sasho MacKenzie's shaft lean variability studies) should produce larger face angle effects for palm versus finger grip configurations \item Control burden: Finger grip users should show lower variability in face angle relative to their variability in applied torques, indicating more effective passive \"filtering\" of variability enumerate Simulation Studies Comprehensive simulation studies could quantify these effects: enumerate \item Build full 3D kinetic model of golfer-club system in MATLAB Simulink \item Define grip angle as a parametric variable (0° = perpendicular to shaft, 90° = parallel to shaft) \item Apply realistic torque profiles to all actuated joints \item Introduce random noise to applied torques \item Measure: itemize \item Constraint torque magnitudes and variability \item Clubhead speed and variability \item Face angle at impact and variability \item Angular accelerations about club axes itemize \item Vary grip angle systematically and assess performance metrics enumerate A key challenge is defining realistic input torques for kinetic simulation. As discussed, this is not straightforward when working from kinematic data, requiring careful decomposition of sensed torques into active and passive components. Experimental Validation Experimental approaches face significant challenges due to the difficulty of measuring constraint torques in vivo. However, indirect validation might be possible through: enumerate \item Performance studies: Compare clubhead speed and face angle variability across grip positions using high-speed motion capture and face impact measurement \item Perturbation studies: Introduce controlled perturbations to forearm rotation and measure resulting face angle effects across different grip configurations \item EMG studies: Assess muscle activation patterns across grip conditions to evaluate control burden \item Inverse dynamics: Use motion capture and force plates to estimate joint torques, comparing sensed torque patterns across grip positions enumerate Extension to Other Joints The constraint torque analysis framework applies to any constrained joint in the kinematic chain: itemize \item Elbow: Often modeled as a hinge joint (one rotational DOF) with constraints on other rotations \item Shoulder complex: Complex multi-axis joint with various constraints depending on model \item Spine: Multiple segments with constrained translations and certain rotations \item Ankle/hip: Lower body joints transmitting ground reaction forces itemize Understanding constraint force/torque transmission throughout the entire kinematic chain could provide a comprehensive framework for optimizing both force generation and control in the golf swing. Relationship to Instructional Practice The \"Grip in the Fingers\" Principle Golf instruction has long emphasized gripping the club \"in the fingers\" rather than \"in the palm.\" This is one of the most consistently taught fundamentals across instructional methods and eras. However, the mechanical basis for this advice has typically been explained through: itemize \item Hand mobility and \"feel\" \item Wrist hinge mechanics \item Leverage considerations \item Empirical observation of skilled players itemize The constraint torque framework provides an additional mechanical explanation: finger grips may be advantageous specifically because they direct uncontrollable, variable constraint torques into an axis where those torques contribute to speed while having minimal impact on face control. This is significant because it suggests the finger grip principle is not just about comfort, feel, or wrist mechanics, but about fundamental force transmission properties of constrained multi-body systems. Individual Variability and Optimization While the analysis predicts general trends, individual optima may vary due to: itemize \item Hand size and finger length \item Wrist anatomy and axis orientations \item Club design (grip thickness, shaft properties) \item Swing style and applied torque patterns \item Skill level and control capabilities itemize The optimal grip angle for a given golfer might be determined through: enumerate \item Measurement of constraint torque variability in their swing \item Assessment of face angle sensitivity to grip changes \item Simulation studies with their specific anthropometry and swing pattern enumerate Limitations of the Analysis Several limitations should be acknowledged: Model Simplification The wrist is more complex than a simple universal joint. Ligamentous constraints, intercarpal joint mechanics, and muscle co-activation all influence behavior. However, the fundamental constraint properties should persist even in more detailed models. Measurement Challenges Direct measurement of constraint torques in vivo is extremely difficult. While simulation provides these values directly, validating them against experimental data requires sophisticated inverse dynamics and careful error analysis. Dynamic Complexity The golf swing involves complex dynamic coupling between all body segments. Isolating the specific effect of wrist constraint torques requires careful experimental design or comprehensive simulation. Proof Limitations As noted in the original hypothesis statement: \"it may be impossible to prove one way or the other.\" The variability and complexity of the system make definitive proof challenging. However, the hypothesis is testable through the predictions it generates. Conclusion This paper proposes a novel mechanical framework for understanding force and torque transmission in the golf swing, focusing on constraint torques at the wrist joint. By modeling the wrist as a universal joint with two actuated and one constrained degree of freedom, we demonstrate that: enumerate \item Universal joints generate constraint torques about constrained axes through the interaction of applied torques, system momentum, and geometric constraints \item These constraint torques provide efficient pathways for force transmission but are inherently variable and uncontrollable \item The angle at which the club is gripped determines whether constraint torques are transmitted into high-inertia axes (promoting speed) or low-inertia axes (increasing face variability) \item A finger grip may be mechanically advantageous because it directs constraint torques into the club's alpha axis, where high inertia filters variability while contributing to clubhead speed \item A palm grip may be disadvantageous because it directs constraint torques into the shaft rotation axis, where low inertia amplifies variability and directly affects face angle \item Arm-club plane separation may provide mechanical advantages related to maintaining optimal constraint torque transmission geometry enumerate This analysis bridges robotics theory (constraint dynamics, universal joint mechanics) and golf biomechanics, providing a rigorous framework for understanding a widely-taught but poorly-understood fundamental principle. While empirical validation presents challenges, the hypothesis generates clear, testable predictions and provides mechanistic insight into force transmission in complex kinematic chains. More broadly, this work illustrates the value of constraint analysis in biomechanics. Constraint forces and torques—often overlooked because they perform no work—play critical roles in force transmission and control. Understanding these passive mechanical pathways provides insight into both optimal technique and the fundamental challenges faced by performers attempting to control complex, nonlinear multi-body systems. The golf swing presents an extraordinary challenge: generating maximum clubhead speed while precisely controlling face orientation using a redundant, nonlinear kinematic chain with multiple passive degrees of freedom. By recognizing how grip orientation influences constraint torque transmission, we gain insight into one mechanism through which skilled performers may simplify this control problem—not through perfect coordination of all variables, but through mechanical configurations that naturally channel variability into performance-irrelevant directions. \section*{Acknowledgments} Thanks to Mike Duffey for insightful discussion regarding the dependence of constraint torques on proximal segment motion. title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
section: 2.1 The Wrist as a Universal Joint
text:
2.1 The Wrist as a Universal Joint
The radiocarpal (wrist) joint exhibits two primary degrees of freedom:

Flexion/Extension: Movement in the sagittal plane relative to the forearm
Radial/Ulnar Deviation: Movement in the frontal plane

These two rotational degrees of freedom occur about approximately perpendicular axes, making the wrist kinematically similar to a universal joint (U-joint) in mechanical systems. The third rotational degree of freedom—forearm pronation/supination—occurs at the radioulnar joints proximal to the wrist, not at the wrist itself.
From a control perspective, muscles can directly generate torques about the flexion/extension and radial/ulnar axes at the wrist. However, rotation about the forearm axis occurs through forearm muscles acting at the proximal radioulnar joint. This configuration is critical: the wrist joint itself has no direct actuation about the forearm rotation axis, making this a constrained rather than actuated degree of freedom at the wrist.

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
text:
3.1 Mechanical Properties of Universal Joints
A universal joint connects two rotating shafts whose axes are perpendicular (or nearly so) and typically intersect. The joint permits rotation about two axes while constraining rotation about a third axis and translation along all axes. This configuration is widely used in mechanical systems—most famously in automotive drive shafts—specifically because of its ability to transmit torque through the constrained rotational axis.
The key property of a universal joint is that torque applied about the longitudinal axis of one shaft is transmitted to the longitudinal axis of the connected shaft through constraint torques rather than through actively applied forces. These constraint torques arise because the joint geometry enforces kinematic constraints; when the system attempts to violate these constraints, reaction forces and torques automatically emerge to maintain the constraints.

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
text:
3.2 Constraint Torques: Definition and Properties
In constrained mechanical systems, the equations of motion can be written in the form:
$\[$
\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{applied}} + \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{constraint}}
\]$$
where:

\(\mathbf{q}\) represents generalized coordinates (joint angles)
\(\mathbf{M}\) is the mass/inertia matrix
\(\mathbf{C}\) contains Coriolis and centrifugal terms
\(\mathbf{G}\) contains gravitational terms
\(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{applied}}\) represents actively applied torques (e.g., from muscles)
\(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{constraint}}\) represents constraint torques maintaining kinematic constraints

The constraint torques can be expressed using Lagrange multipliers:
$\[$
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{constraint}} = \mathbf{J}^T(\mathbf{q})\boldsymbol{\lambda}
\]$$
where \(\mathbf{J}\) is the constraint Jacobian matrix and \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) is the vector of Lagrange multipliers. These constraint torques have several important properties:

No mechanical work: Constraint torques act in directions where motion is prevented, so they perform no work: \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{constraint}} \cdot \dot{\mathbf{q}} = 0\)
Force transmission: Despite doing no work, constraint torques efficiently transmit forces between segments
Nonlinearity: Constraint torques depend nonlinearly on system configuration, velocities, and applied torques
Uncontrollability: Because they arise from constraints rather than actuation, constraint torques cannot be directly controlled
Variability: The dependence on multiple system states makes constraint torques inherently variable

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
section: 3.3 Constraint Torques in Forward Dynamics Simulation
text:
3.3 Constraint Torques in Forward Dynamics Simulation
In MATLAB Simulink’s Simscape Multibody environment, joint blocks allow specification of input torques and sensing of output torques. For a universal joint driven by input torques about its two actuated axes, the sensed output torques include three components:
$\[$ egin{aligned}
\tau_{\text{sensed},x} &= \tau_{x,\text{applied}} + \tau_{x,\text{passive}} \\
\tau_{\text{sensed},y} &= \tau_{y,\text{applied}} + \tau_{y,\text{passive}} \\
\tau_{\text{sensed},z} &= \tau_{z,\text{constraint}}
\end{aligned}\]$$
where:

Subscripts \(x\) and \(y\) represent the two actuated axes (e.g., flexion/extension and radial/ulnar)
Subscript \(z\) represents the constrained axis (forearm rotation)
\(\tau_{\text{passive}}\) represents passive dynamic effects (inertial, Coriolis, etc.)
\(\tau_{\text{constraint}}\) is the constraint torque about the constrained axis

The presence of \(\tau_{z,\text{constraint}} \neq 0\) despite no direct actuation about the \(z\)-axis is the signature of constraint torque generation. This torque emerges from the interaction of:

Applied torques about the actuated axes
System momentum and inertial effects
Joint geometry and constraint equations
Configuration-dependent coupling between axes

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
section: 3.4 Physical Demonstration of Constraint Torque Generation
text:
3.4 Physical Demonstration of Constraint Torque Generation
The generation of constraint torques at a universal joint can be demonstrated with a simple physical experiment:

Grasp your left wrist firmly with your right hand
Actively prevent any forearm rotation (pronation/supination)
With your left hand, simultaneously apply:

Flexion torque (curling palm toward forearm)
Ulnar deviation torque (moving hand toward pinky side)

Observe the rotational force felt by the restraining right hand

The torque felt by the right hand about the forearm rotation axis is a constraint torque. It arises not from any muscular effort to rotate the forearm, but from the simultaneous application of torques about the two perpendicular wrist axes. The right hand must apply an equal and opposite constraint torque to maintain the no-rotation constraint.
This demonstration reveals an important principle: constraint torques can be generated through coordinated actuation of permitted degrees of freedom, even though the constrained degree of freedom cannot be directly actuated at that joint.

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
section: 4.1 The Wrist as a Torque Transmission Pathway
text:
4.1 The Wrist as a Torque Transmission Pathway
In the golf swing, torques generated by proximal segments (trunk rotation, shoulder internal rotation, forearm pronation) must be transmitted to the club. The wrist joint, positioned between the forearm and hand, serves as a critical link in this transmission chain.
The constraint torque property of universal joints provides an elegant mechanism for this transmission. Torque about the forearm rotation axis (generated by forearm pronation/supination muscles) can be transmitted through the wrist to the hand without requiring wrist muscles to actively generate this torque. The constraint properties of the joint handle the transmission automatically.
However, this passive transmission comes with a critical caveat: because constraint torques cannot be directly controlled at the wrist, they inherit all the variability present in the proximal segments that generate them. As noted in discussion of this phenomenon:

“\[
Constraint torques
\] are dependent on motion of other components—any rotation or torque in the forearm will directly affect these and there are no degrees of freedom in the wrist to modulate or control any of these torques induced from the forearm axis. It is forced to transmit whatever it receives on the rotational axis.”

This creates a control challenge: the wrist transmits constraint torques from proximal segments to the club, but has no mechanism to filter or modulate these torques. Whatever variability exists in forearm motion, trunk rotation, or their interaction will be transmitted directly through the wrist via constraint torques.

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
section: 4.2 Variability Accumulation Through the Kinematic Chain
text:
4.2 Variability Accumulation Through the Kinematic Chain
The constraint torques measured at the wrist include contributions from variability in:

Shoulder motion: Variations in shoulder internal/external rotation timing and magnitude
Forearm rotation: Variability in pronation/supination velocity and acceleration
Wrist actuation: Variations in flexion/extension and radial/ulnar deviation torques
Dynamic coupling: Nonlinear interactions between all segment motions
System configuration: Dependence on instantaneous joint angles throughout the chain

Because the wrist cannot modulate constraint torques, it effectively acts as a passive transmission mechanism that accumulates variability from all upstream sources. The critical question then becomes: where do these variable constraint torques go?
The answer depends critically on the angle at which the club is gripped relative to the wrist joint axes.

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
text:
5.1 Coordinate System Definitions
To analyze grip angle effects, we must define coordinate systems for the relevant segments:

5.1.0.1 Wrist coordinate system:

\(x\)-axis: Flexion/extension rotation axis (approximately dorsal-palmar direction)
\(y\)-axis: Radial/ulnar deviation axis (approximately medial-lateral direction)
\(z\)-axis: Constrained axis (approximately aligned with forearm long axis)



5.1.0.2 Club coordinate system:

Shaft axis: Along the club shaft from grip to clubhead
Alpha axis: Perpendicular to shaft, in the swing plane (controls in-plane angular motion)
Beta axis: Perpendicular to shaft, perpendicular to swing plane (controls face rotation)

Near impact, when the club shaft is roughly aligned with the forearm, these coordinate systems have a particular relationship. However, the critical parameter is how the hand coordinate system (distal end of the wrist universal joint) aligns with the club coordinate system, which depends on grip position.

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
section: 5.2 Case 1: Grip in the Fingers (Deep Grip)
text:
5.2 Case 1: Grip in the Fingers (Deep Grip)
When the club is gripped predominantly in the fingers:

The butt of the club sits below the heel of the palm
The shaft passes through or near the base of the fingers
The hand’s \(z\)-axis (emerging from the wrist constraint torques) is approximately perpendicular to the shaft

In this configuration, constraint torques transmitted through the wrist’s constrained axis are directed approximately along the club’s alpha axis—the axis of in-plane rotational motion. The alpha axis has high moment of inertia because it represents rotation that moves the clubhead through its maximum radius of gyration.
The angular acceleration produced by a constraint torque \(\tau_c\) about the alpha axis is:
$\[$
\alpha_{\text{swing plane}} = \frac{\tau_c}{I_{\alpha}}
\]$$
where \(I_{\alpha}\) is the club’s moment of inertia about the alpha axis (typically 0.004-0.006 kgÂ·mÂ² for drivers).
Because \(I_{\alpha}\) is large, even substantial constraint torques produce relatively modest angular accelerations. More importantly, rotation about the alpha axis produces translation of the clubhead through the impact zone—the very motion we want for generating clubhead speed. The constraint torques are channeled into productive work.
Furthermore, face angle is minimally affected by alpha axis rotation near impact (when the shaft is near the ball). The relationship between alpha rotation and face angle change is approximately:
$\[$
\Delta \theta_{\text{face}} \approx \Delta \alpha \cdot \sin(\text{shaft angle})
\]$$
Near impact, shaft angle is small, so \(\sin(\text{shaft angle}) \approx 0\), making face angle relatively insensitive to alpha axis rotation.

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
section: 5.3 Case 2: Grip in the Palm (Shallow Grip)
text:
5.3 Case 2: Grip in the Palm (Shallow Grip)
When the butt of the club extends into the palm:

The butt of the club sits in or near the heel of the palm
The shaft passes through or above the base of the fingers
The hand’s \(z\)-axis is more closely aligned with the shaft axis

In this configuration, constraint torques transmitted through the wrist are directed more closely along the club’s beta axis—the shaft rotation axis that controls face angle. This axis has low moment of inertia (typically 0.0001-0.0002 kgÂ·mÂ² about shaft rotation).
The angular acceleration produced by the same constraint torque \(\tau_c\) is now:
$\[$
\alpha_{\text{face rotation}} = \frac{\tau_c}{I_{\beta}}
\]$$
where \(I_{\beta} \ll I_{\alpha}\). The ratio is typically:
$\[$
\frac{I_{\alpha}}{I_{\beta}} \approx 20-30
\]$$
This means the same magnitude of constraint torque produces 20-30 times greater angular acceleration when directed into face rotation versus swing plane rotation. Moreover, face rotation directly controls clubface orientation—the variable most critical for shot dispersion.

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
text:
5.4 Implications for Speed and Consistency
The grip angle hypothesis predicts fundamentally different outcomes for the two grip configurations:

5.4.0.1 Finger Grip (Perpendicular to Shaft):

Constraint torques directed into high-inertia alpha axis
Variable constraint torques produce modest, bounded angular accelerations
Alpha rotation contributes to clubhead translation and speed
Face angle remains relatively stable despite constraint torque variability
Lower control burden: variability is channeled into performance-relevant direction



5.4.0.2 Palm Grip (Aligned with Shaft):

Constraint torques directed into low-inertia beta axis
Variable constraint torques produce large angular accelerations
Beta rotation contributes primarily to face rotation, not clubhead speed
Face angle highly sensitive to constraint torque variability
Higher control burden: precise coordination required to manage face angle

The fundamental trade-off is between an axis where constraint torques are useful but less variable in their effect (alpha) versus an axis where constraint torques are amplified and directly affect the critical performance variable (beta).

title: Constraint Torques at the Wrist: How Grip Angle Influences Force Transmission and Face Angle Variability in the Golf Swing
text:
5.5 Quantitative Example
Consider a constraint torque with standard deviation \(\sigma_{\tau_c} = 5\) NÂ·m transmitted through the wrist during the downswing. For a finger grip directing this into the alpha axis:
$\[$ egin{aligned}
\sigma_{\alpha} &= \frac{\sigma_{\tau_c}}{I_{\alpha}} = \frac{5 \text{ NÂ·m}}{0.005 \text{ kgÂ·m}^2} = 1000 \text{ rad/s}^2 \\
\sigma_{\theta} &\approx \sigma_{\alpha} \cdot \Delta t \approx 1000 \times 0.05 = 50 \text{ rad/s}
\end{aligned}\]$$
This angular velocity variation in the swing plane contributes to clubhead speed variation but has minimal effect on face angle near impact.
For a palm grip directing the same torque into the beta axis:
$\[$ egin{aligned}
\sigma_{\beta} &= \frac{\sigma_{\tau_c}}{I_{\beta}} = \frac{5 \text{ NÂ·m}}{0.00015 \text{ kgÂ·m}^2} = 33,333 \text{ rad/s}^2 \\
\sigma_{\omega_{\text{face}}} &\approx \sigma_{\beta} \cdot \Delta t \approx 33,333 \times 0.05 = 1667 \text{ rad/s}
\end{aligned}\]$$
This face rotation rate variation translates directly to face angle variation at impact. Over a 50 ms window near impact:
$\[$
\sigma_{\text{face angle}} \approx 1667 \text{ rad/s} \times 0.05 \text{ s} \approx 83 \text{ rad} \approx 4.8Â°
\]$$
This example illustrates how identical constraint torque variability produces dramatically different outcomes depending on grip orientation.

\tau_{\text{sensed},z} &= \tau_{\text{constraint},z}
\end{aligned}\]$$
The \(z\)-component is purely constraint torque (no actuation exists). But the \(x\) and \(y\) components include passive dynamic terms that arise from motion, not from actuation. Separating these requires detailed knowledge of the system dynamics—exactly the topic addressed in robotics courses on constrained dynamics.

section: 7.2 Constraint Forces in the Equations of Motion
text:
7.2 Constraint Forces in the Equations of Motion
For a holonomic constraint (one expressible as a function of positions): $\[$
\phi(\mathbf{q}) = 0
\]$$
The constraint force/torque is: $\[$
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{constraint}} = \mathbf{J}^T(\mathbf{q})\boldsymbol{\lambda}
\]$$
where the constraint Jacobian is: $\[$
\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial \mathbf{q}}
\]$$
The Lagrange multipliers \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) are determined by enforcing the constraint at the acceleration level: $\[$
\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \dot{\mathbf{J}}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} = 0
\]$$
For a universal joint constraining rotation about the \(z\)-axis and all translations, the constraint equations and resulting constraint torques involve complex geometric relationships between segment orientations and the joint constraint structure.
Fortunately, MATLAB Simulink computes these constraint torques automatically and provides them as sensed outputs. This removes the burden of manual calculation but requires understanding what these values represent and how they emerge from system dynamics.

8.1 Testable Predictions
The grip angle hypothesis generates several testable predictions:

Face angle variability: Golfers using palm grips should exhibit greater face angle variability at impact compared to finger grip users, even with similar overall swing kinematics
Constraint torque magnitude: Forward dynamics simulations with different grip angles should show that identical applied torques produce different constraint torque distributions depending on grip configuration
Clubhead speed: For the same applied torques and overall swing kinematics, finger grips should produce higher clubhead speeds due to more efficient channeling of constraint torques into translational motion
Variability sensitivity: Introducing random noise into applied torques (as in Sasho MacKenzie’s shaft lean variability studies) should produce larger face angle effects for palm versus finger grip configurations
Control burden: Finger grip users should show lower variability in face angle relative to their variability in applied torques, indicating more effective passive “filtering” of variability

A key challenge is defining realistic input torques for kinetic simulation. As discussed, this is not straightforward when working from kinematic data, requiring careful decomposition of sensed torques into active and passive components.

8.3 Experimental Validation
Experimental approaches face significant challenges due to the difficulty of measuring constraint torques in vivo. However, indirect validation might be possible through:

Performance studies: Compare clubhead speed and face angle variability across grip positions using high-speed motion capture and face impact measurement
Perturbation studies: Introduce controlled perturbations to forearm rotation and measure resulting face angle effects across different grip configurations
EMG studies: Assess muscle activation patterns across grip conditions to evaluate control burden
Inverse dynamics: Use motion capture and force plates to estimate joint torques, comparing sensed torque patterns across grip positions

text:
8.4 Extension to Other Joints
The constraint torque analysis framework applies to any constrained joint in the kinematic chain:

Elbow: Often modeled as a hinge joint (one rotational DOF) with constraints on other rotations
Shoulder complex: Complex multi-axis joint with various constraints depending on model
Spine: Multiple segments with constrained translations and certain rotations
Ankle/hip: Lower body joints transmitting ground reaction forces

Understanding constraint force/torque transmission throughout the entire kinematic chain could provide a comprehensive framework for optimizing both force generation and control in the golf swing.

9.1 The “Grip in the Fingers” Principle
Golf instruction has long emphasized gripping the club “in the fingers” rather than “in the palm.” This is one of the most consistently taught fundamentals across instructional methods and eras. However, the mechanical basis for this advice has typically been explained through:

Hand mobility and “feel”
Wrist hinge mechanics
Leverage considerations
Empirical observation of skilled players

The constraint torque framework provides an additional mechanical explanation: finger grips may be advantageous specifically because they direct uncontrollable, variable constraint torques into an axis where those torques contribute to speed while having minimal impact on face control.
This is significant because it suggests the finger grip principle is not just about comfort, feel, or wrist mechanics, but about fundamental force transmission properties of constrained multi-body systems.

9.2 Individual Variability and Optimization
While the analysis predicts general trends, individual optima may vary due to:

Hand size and finger length
Wrist anatomy and axis orientations
Club design (grip thickness, shaft properties)
Swing style and applied torque patterns
Skill level and control capabilities

The optimal grip angle for a given golfer might be determined through:

Measurement of constraint torque variability in their swing
Assessment of face angle sensitivity to grip changes
Simulation studies with their specific anthropometry and swing pattern

text:
9.3 Limitations of the Analysis
Several limitations should be acknowledged:

9.3.0.1 Model Simplification
The wrist is more complex than a simple universal joint. Ligamentous constraints, intercarpal joint mechanics, and muscle co-activation all influence behavior. However, the fundamental constraint properties should persist even in more detailed models.


9.3.0.2 Measurement Challenges
Direct measurement of constraint torques in vivo is extremely difficult. While simulation provides these values directly, validating them against experimental data requires sophisticated inverse dynamics and careful error analysis.


9.3.0.3 Dynamic Complexity
The golf swing involves complex dynamic coupling between all body segments. Isolating the specific effect of wrist constraint torques requires careful experimental design or comprehensive simulation.


9.3.0.4 Proof Limitations
As noted in the original hypothesis statement: “it may be impossible to prove one way or the other.” The variability and complexity of the system make definitive proof challenging. However, the hypothesis is testable through the predictions it generates.
